pages.name: One part, several views
pages.text: A part is solid, but a sheet is flat. One picture of a part can hide what lies behind it. So a drawing shows the part from several sides, each seen square-on. Here the bracket is turned to show its upright with the hole, its base with the slot, and the rib between them.
pages.alt: A small steel bracket in a glass box, seen from the front left. It has a flat base with a slot down through it, an upright along the back with a hole through it, and a thin rib in the corner between them.

pages.name: What a view loses
pages.task: You look square at the front of the bracket. Which of its sizes does the front view not show?
pages.why: Looking square-on, every point along your line of sight lands on the same spot. So the depth folds away. A view keeps two of the three sizes. That is why a drawing usually needs at least two views.
pages.alt: The bracket seen from the front left, above, with an arrow showing you look square at its front. Beside it is its front view: an outline 80 wide and 60 high, the hole as a circle, the rib, and the slot's ends as dashed lines in the base. An arrow along the bracket marks its depth, front to back, which the front view does not show.

pages.name: Unfold the box: first angle
pages.text: Picture the bracket inside a glass box. In first angle, each view is cast onto the wall behind the part, on the far side from you. Open the box out flat, and the view from above lands below the front view. The box lies open and flat. The front view is in the middle. The view from above is below it. The view from the left end is on its right. The first-angle symbol sits in a corner.
pages.alt: A first-angle sheet of the bracket: the front view, with the view from above below the front view and the view from the left end to the right of the front view. Above the sheet is a small copy of the bracket you can turn.

pages.name: Where does it go?
pages.task: The sheet uses first angle. You look at the bracket from its left end. Where does that view go?
pages.answer: To the right of the front view
pages.why: From the left end, the view falls on the wall to the right of the part. Open the box flat and that wall lies to the right of the front view. The end view lines up with the front view and shares its height.
pages.alt: A first-angle sheet of the bracket: the front view, with the view from above below the front view and the view from the left end to the right of the front view. Above the sheet is a small copy of the bracket you can turn.
options: To the left of the front view
To the right of the front view

pages.name: The other rule
pages.text: Third angle draws each view on the wall between you and the part. So the view from above sits above the front view instead. The projection symbol names the rule. It is a cone, drawn by that rule. In first angle, its circles sit by the cone's wide end. In third angle, they sit by its narrow end. The third-angle sheet sits with the first-angle one. In third angle, the view from above is above the front view. The view from the left end is on its left. Each sheet has its own symbol.
pages.alt: A first-angle sheet of the bracket: the front view, with the view from above below the front view and the view from the left end to the right of the front view. A third-angle sheet of the bracket: the front view, with the view from above above the front view and the view from the left end to the left of the front view.

pages.name: Read the symbol
pages.task: Read this sheet's projection symbol. A view of the bracket sits to the right of the front view. Which side was it seen from?
pages.why: The circles sit by the cone's narrow end, so the sheet is third angle. Third angle draws each view on the wall between you and the part. Seen from the right end, that wall is on the right. Opened flat, it stays on the right.
pages.alt: A third-angle sheet of the bracket: the front view, with the view from the right end to the right of the front view. Above the sheet is a small copy of the bracket you can turn.

pages.name: Lines that mean something
pages.text: A thick solid line is an edge you can see. A dashed line is an edge hidden inside or behind the part. A thin chain line marks the centre of a hole or slot. It runs long, short, long. In the front view, the two short dashed lines in the base are lit. On the bracket, the slot's ends light up inside the base.
pages.alt: A first-angle sheet of the bracket: the front view, with the view from above below the front view and the view from the left end to the right of the front view. Above the sheet is a small copy of the bracket you can turn. One line is lit, with its edge lit on the bracket.

pages.name: Sketch it
pages.task: On paper, sketch the bracket seen from above. How does the hole through the upright show in that view?
pages.answer: Two dashed lines, with a chain line between
pages.why: From above, you look down onto the upright's top face. The hole runs front to back underneath it. Its sides are edges hidden behind material, so they are dashed. The chain line marks its centre.
pages.alt: A first-angle sheet of the bracket: the front view, with the view from above below the front view and the view from the left end to the right of the front view. Above the sheet is a small copy of the bracket you can turn.
options: Two dashed lines, with a chain line between

pages.name: Cut it open
pages.text: To show the inside, picture the part cut along a plane, with the near piece lifted away. A chain line, thick at its ends, marks the cut. Its arrows show which way you look. The section view hatches each cut face with thin sloping lines. A rib cut along its length is left plain. The plane cuts through the hole. In section A–A, the base and the upright are hatched. The upright has a gap where the hole is.
pages.alt: A first-angle sheet of the bracket: the front view, with the view from above below the front view and section A–A to the right of the front view. Above the sheet is a small copy of the bracket you can turn. A cutting plane through the bracket shows as a chain line on the front view, 20 from its left end.

pages.name: Hatched or plain
pages.task: The plane now runs down the middle of the rib. Which cut faces are hatched in section A–A?
pages.answer: The base and the upright only
pages.why: Hatched, the rib would make the corner look solid, as if the metal were thick there. Left plain, with its outline drawn, it reads as a thin rib.
pages.alt: A first-angle sheet of the bracket: the front view, with the view from above below the front view and section A–A to the right of the front view. Above the sheet is a small copy of the bracket you can turn. A cutting plane through the bracket shows as a chain line on the front view, 40 from its left end.
options: The base, the upright and the rib
The base and the upright only

pages.name: Sizes, limits and scale
pages.text: Work to the sizes written on the drawing, here in millimetres. A size of 25 ± 0.1 means any length from 24.9 to 25.1 mm is right. The scale 1 : 5 says the picture is drawn a fifth of the part's size. The slot's length is lit. Its limits, 24.9 and 25.1 mm, sit beside it. The title block shows the scale, the units, the projection symbol, the drawing number and its issue letter.
pages.alt: A first-angle sheet of the bracket: the front view, with the view from above below the front view and the view from the left end to the right of the front view. Above the sheet is a small copy of the bracket you can turn. Sizes are written on in millimetres, with a title block along the bottom.

pages.name: The smallest that passes
pages.task: The hole's centre is 40 ± 0.2 above the base's underside. What is the smallest height that still passes?
pages.why: The smallest that passes is 40 − 0.2, which is 39.8 mm. The largest is 40 + 0.2, which is 40.2 mm.
pages.alt: A first-angle sheet of the bracket: the front view, with the view from above below the front view and the view from the left end to the right of the front view. Above the sheet is a small copy of the bracket you can turn. Sizes are written on in millimetres, with a title block along the bottom.

pages.name: Drawn to scale
pages.task: The base is 80 long. The scale is 1 : 5. How long is the base drawn on the sheet?
pages.why: 80 ÷ 5 is 16 mm. Still work to the written 80. It is the part's true size.
pages.alt: A first-angle sheet of the bracket: the front view, with the view from above below the front view and the view from the left end to the right of the front view. Above the sheet is a small copy of the bracket you can turn. Sizes are written on in millimetres, with a title block along the bottom.

pages.name: Which part?
pages.task: Which part do these views show?
pages.why: From above, the feature is a circle, so it is round. In the front view, its sides are dashed and stay within the base. So it is a hole through the base. It takes both views to tell.
pages.alt: A first-angle sheet of a second bracket: its front view, with two dashed lines and a chain line in the base, and its view from above below it, with a solid circle and crossed chain lines in the base. Below are three small parts: Part A with a slot through its base, Part B with a round hole down through its base, and Part C with a round peg standing on its base.
